courses.title: 19. AVR registers and your first instructions
courses.summary: Meet the AVR8 register file and load, copy and observe 8-bit values with LDI and MOV.
courses.asm:
; Load three registers and copy one
ldi r16, 0x2A   ; 42
ldi r17, 0b1010 ; 10
mov r18, r16    ; copy r16 into r18
out PORTB, r18  ; observe 0x2A on PORTB

lessons.title: 32 general-purpose registers
paragraphs: The AVR8 CPU has 32 one-byte registers, R0–R31, wired directly to the ALU. Nearly every instruction reads and writes these registers in a single clock cycle.
Registers R16–R31 are the 'high' half: only they accept the immediate instructions such as LDI, ANDI and SUBI. Keep working values in R16–R31 to avoid 'needs a high register' errors.
lessons.example:
ldi r16, 200   ; ok
ldi r2, 200    ; error: LDI needs R16-R31
lessons.pitfall: LDI, SUBI, ANDI, ORI, CPI and SER only work on R16–R31; the low registers R0–R15 cannot take an immediate.

question.prompt: Which register can receive an LDI immediate?
question.explanation: LDI targets the high registers R16–R31; r20 qualifies.

lessons.title: LDI: load an immediate
paragraphs: LDI Rd, K places the constant K (0–255) into a high register in one cycle. Constants may be decimal (42), hex (0x2A) or binary (0b00101010).
LDI is how every program seeds its working values before arithmetic begins.
lessons.pitfall: An immediate must fit in a byte (0–255). ldi r16, 300 is an assembly error.

question.prompt: After `ldi r17, 0b1010`, what is r17 in decimal?

lessons.title: MOV and observing values
paragraphs: MOV Rd, Rr copies one register into another without changing flags. It is the register-to-register move; use it to duplicate a value before you destroy it.
This lab observes a byte by writing it to PORTB with OUT; the simulator records each PORTB write so you can see your result.
lessons.example:
mov r18, r16  ; r18 now equals r16
out PORTB, r18
lessons.pitfall: MOV does not touch the SREG flags, so you cannot branch on a MOV; compare first.

question.prompt: What does MOV change besides the destination register?

lessons.title: Decimal, hex and binary
paragraphs: AVR tools show bytes in hex because each hex digit is exactly four bits. 0x2A is 0010 1010, which is 42 decimal.
Reading registers in hex makes bit patterns obvious, which matters once you start masking and shifting bits.
lessons.pitfall: A leading zero does not make a number octal here; 010 is ten, not eight.

question.prompt: 0xFF as decimal is:

steps: Assemble the preset and read the opcode listing beside each line.
Run it and confirm r16, r17 and r18 in the register panel.
Change the LDI value and re-run; watch PORTB and the listing update.
Add a MOV that duplicates r17 into r19 and verify it.

bridge.principle: Registers are the CPU's fastest storage; everything flows through them.
bridge.minecraft: Think of each register as a labelled chest the ALU can reach in one tick.
bridge.other: The same program runs on a real ATmega with avr-gcc/avra and avrdude, or under simulavr; the mnemonics and flags are identical to this subset.

acceptance: Use only LDI and MOV

No assembly errors in the listing

questions.prompt: How many general-purpose registers does the AVR8 have?
Which instruction copies r5 into r6?
questions.explanation: MOV Rd,Rr copies Rr into Rd.

courses.title: 20. AVR arithmetic and the status register
courses.summary: Add and subtract bytes with ADD, SUB, INC and DEC and read the carry, zero, negative and overflow flags.
courses.asm:
; Add two bytes and watch the flags
ldi r16, 0x80
ldi r17, 0x80
add r16, r17   ; 0x80+0x80 = 0x00 with carry, zero and overflow set
out PORTB, r16

lessons.title: ADD and ADC
paragraphs: ADD Rd, Rr adds two registers and stores the sum in Rd, updating the flags. ADC adds with the carry flag, which is how you chain bytes into 16-bit sums.
After ADD, the carry flag C is set when the unsigned result exceeded 255.
lessons.pitfall: ADD overwrites Rd. Copy the operand with MOV first if you still need the original.

question.prompt: Which instruction continues a multi-byte addition using the carry?

lessons.title: SUB, SUBI and compare
paragraphs: SUB Rd, Rr subtracts; SUBI Rd, K subtracts an immediate (high registers only). The carry flag after a subtraction means a borrow occurred (the unsigned result went negative).
CP and CPI subtract but store nothing — they exist purely to set flags before a branch.
lessons.example:
subi r16, 1   ; r16 = r16 - 1
cp r16, r17   ; set flags for r16 - r17, discard result
lessons.pitfall: After subtraction C=1 means 'borrow', i.e. the first operand was smaller.

question.prompt: What does CP store?

lessons.title: The SREG flags
paragraphs: The status register SREG holds C (carry), Z (zero), N (negative, bit 7 of the result), V (two's-complement overflow) and S (sign = N xor V), among others.
Zero means the result byte was 0. Overflow means a signed result wrapped past +127 or −128.
lessons.example:
ldi r16,0x80
ldi r17,0x80
add r16,r17  ; Z=1, C=1, V=1
lessons.pitfall: C is for unsigned overflow; V is for signed overflow. They are different flags for different interpretations.

question.prompt: Which flag signals a signed overflow?
question.explanation: V is the two's-complement overflow flag.

lessons.title: INC and DEC
paragraphs: INC and DEC add or subtract one and update Z, N, V and S — but deliberately leave the carry flag C unchanged, so you can count inside a carry-sensitive loop.
DEC reaching zero sets Z, which is the classic way to end a countdown loop with BRNE.
lessons.example:
ldi r16, 3
dec r16   ; 2, Z=0
dec r16   ; 1
dec r16   ; 0, Z=1
lessons.pitfall: INC/DEC do NOT affect carry; do not rely on C after them.

question.prompt: Which flag does DEC leave unchanged?
question.explanation: INC and DEC do not touch the carry flag.

steps: Run the preset and read every SREG flag after the ADD.
Change r17 to 0x01 and predict C, Z and V before re-running.
Replace ADD with SUB and explain the new carry meaning.
Build a three-step countdown with DEC and watch Z.
courses.expected: r16 = 0x00; SREG shows C=1, Z=1, V=1, N=0, S=1; PORTB = 0.

bridge.principle: Flags are the CPU's memory of the last result; branches read them.
bridge.minecraft: A redstone comparator reacts to a signal the way a branch reacts to a flag.
bridge.other: The same program runs on a real ATmega with avr-gcc/avra and avrdude, or under simulavr; the mnemonics and flags are identical to this subset.

challenge.task: Compute 200 + 100 across the carry into a second register.
acceptance: Use ADD then ADC
The high byte becomes 1
Explain why the low byte is 44

questions.prompt: `ldi r16,0xFF` then `ldi r17,1` then `add r16,r17` sets which flags?
questions.explanation: 255+1 wraps to 0 with a carry out.
S = N ⊕ V, the signed comparison result.

questions.prompt: DEC is most often paired with:
questions.explanation: DEC then BRNE forms a countdown loop.

questions.prompt: To add a with-carry high byte you use:
questions.explanation: ADC chains the carry into the next byte.

courses.title: 21. AVR logic, masking and shifts
courses.summary: Use AND, OR, EOR, COM and the shift/rotate instructions to set, clear, test and move bits.
courses.asm:
; Mask, set and shift bits
ldi r16, 0b1100
andi r16, 0b1010  ; keep common bits -> 0b1000
ori  r16, 0b0001  ; set bit0 -> 0b1001
lsl  r16          ; shift left -> 0b10010
out PORTB, r16

lessons.title: AND/OR/EOR masking
paragraphs: ANDI clears the bits that are 0 in the mask (keep only selected bits); ORI sets the bits that are 1 in the mask; EOR toggles bits. Logic instructions clear the V flag and set N, Z and S.
Masking is how firmware changes one pin without disturbing the others in a port.
lessons.example:
andi r16, 0b00001111  ; keep low nibble
ori  r16, 0b10000000  ; set bit 7
lessons.pitfall: AND with a mask of 0 clears everything; that is CLR (or EOR Rd,Rd), not a mistake to make by accident.

question.prompt: To force bit 3 high without changing other bits you use:

lessons.title: COM, NEG and CLR/SER
paragraphs: COM forms the one's complement (flip every bit) and sets carry; NEG forms the two's complement (arithmetic negation). CLR zeroes a register, SER sets it to 0xFF.
These are the quickest ways to invert or preset a byte.
lessons.example:
ldi r16, 0x0F
com r16   ; 0xF0
neg r16   ; 0x10
lessons.pitfall: COM is bitwise NOT; NEG is arithmetic −x. They differ by one (COM x = NEG x − 1).

question.prompt: COM r16 turns 0x0F into:

lessons.title: LSL, LSR, ROL, ROR, ASR
paragraphs: LSL shifts left (×2) pushing bit 7 into carry; LSR shifts right (÷2 unsigned) pushing bit 0 into carry. ROL/ROR rotate through the carry, and ASR shifts right keeping the sign bit.
Shifting is cheap multiplication and division by powers of two.
lessons.example:
lsl r16  ; r16 = r16*2, C = old bit7
lsr r16  ; r16 = r16/2, C = old bit0
lessons.pitfall: LSR is an unsigned divide; use ASR to divide a signed value by two.

question.prompt: LSL r16 is equivalent to:
question.explanation: A left shift multiplies by two.

lessons.title: SWAP and nibbles
paragraphs: SWAP exchanges the high and low nibbles of a register in one cycle, which is handy for packing two 4-bit values or formatting hex output.
Combined with ANDI it extracts either nibble.
lessons.example:
ldi r16, 0x4C
swap r16  ; 0xC4
lessons.pitfall: SWAP changes no flags; it is a pure nibble exchange.

question.prompt: SWAP of 0x4C is:

steps: Run the preset and watch r16 after each logic step.
Change the AND mask and predict which bits survive.
Replace LSL with LSR and read the carry it produces.
Use SWAP then ANDI to isolate the high nibble of 0x4C.
courses.expected: r16 ends 0b00010010 (0x12); AND then OR then LSL applied in order.

bridge.principle: Boolean masks let one instruction edit chosen bits.
bridge.minecraft: An AND mask is a row of redstone AND gates selecting lines.
bridge.other: The same program runs on a real ATmega with avr-gcc/avra and avrdude, or under simulavr; the mnemonics and flags are identical to this subset.

challenge.task: Clear the low nibble of a byte while keeping the high nibble.

Mask value is 0xF0
Show the before and after in PORTB

questions.explanation: Bits set in the mask are kept.
XOR with itself is zero (that is CLR).

questions.prompt: Which instruction divides an unsigned byte by two?
questions.explanation: LSR shifts right, dividing by two.

questions.prompt: LSL pushes which bit into carry?
questions.explanation: The top bit shifts out into C.

courses.title: 22. AVR comparisons, branches and loops
courses.summary: Turn flags into control flow with CP/CPI and the conditional branches, and build counted and conditional loops.
courses.asm:
; Sum 1..5 with a counted loop
ldi r16, 0    ; accumulator
ldi r17, 1    ; value
ldi r18, 5    ; counter
loop:
  add r16, r17
  inc r17
  dec r18
  brne loop   ; repeat until counter hits zero
out PORTB, r16  ; 15

lessons.title: CP, CPI and the comparison flags
paragraphs: CP Rd, Rr and CPI Rd, K subtract to set flags without storing a result. The branches then read those flags: Z for equality, C for unsigned ordering, and S for signed ordering.
Always compare immediately before the branch; any flag-changing instruction in between invalidates the test.
lessons.example:
cpi r16, 10
brlo lower   ; branch if r16 < 10 (unsigned)
lessons.pitfall: An INC, ADD or LDI between the CP and the branch rewrites the flags you meant to test.

question.prompt: Which flag does BREQ test?

lessons.title: Conditional branches
paragraphs: BREQ/BRNE test zero; BRCS/BRCC (also BRLO/BRSH) test carry for unsigned <, ≥; BRLT/BRGE test the S flag for signed <, ≥; BRMI/BRPL test the sign bit.
A branch is a short relative jump: it is taken only when its flag condition holds, otherwise execution falls through.
lessons.example:
brne loop   ; if Z=0, jump back to loop
brsh big    ; if unsigned >= , jump
lessons.pitfall: Use BRLO/BRSH for unsigned values and BRLT/BRGE for signed; mixing them gives wrong results near 0x80.

question.prompt: For unsigned 'less than', branch with:
question.explanation: BRLO (=BRCS) is the unsigned less-than branch.

lessons.title: Counted loops
paragraphs: The idiomatic AVR loop loads a counter, does work, DECs the counter and uses BRNE to repeat until it reaches zero. DEC sets Z without touching carry, so carry-based work inside the loop still behaves.
RJMP provides the unconditional jump for the top of a while-style loop.
lessons.example:
ldi r18, 5
loop:
  dec r18
  brne loop
lessons.pitfall: Forgetting to DEC (or DECing the wrong register) makes an infinite loop; the simulator stops at its step limit.

question.prompt: What ends a `dec`/`brne` countdown?

options.text: Z set when the counter hits 0

question.explanation: BRNE falls through when DEC makes the counter zero.

lessons.title: RJMP and structure
paragraphs: RJMP label is an unconditional relative jump. Combined with a comparison and a conditional branch it builds if/else and while structures out of flat instructions.
Labels are resolved by the assembler to a signed offset; the listing shows the encoded branch word.
lessons.example:
rjmp done
...
done:
  nop
lessons.pitfall: A relative branch only reaches ±64 words; a far target needs RJMP (±2k) or a restructure.

question.prompt: RJMP is:

steps: Run the 1..5 sum and confirm r16 = 15.
Step the loop and watch r18 fall to zero and Z flip.
Change the counter to 10 and predict the new sum.
Rewrite the loop to stop with CPI r17, 6 and BRSH.
courses.expected: r16 = 15 (1+2+3+4+5); the loop runs five times and ends with Z set.

bridge.minecraft: A comparator plus a repeater is a flag plus a branch.
bridge.other: The same program runs on a real ATmega with avr-gcc/avra and avrdude, or under simulavr; the mnemonics and flags are identical to this subset.

courses.title: 23. AVR data memory, pointers and the stack
courses.summary: Move bytes to and from SRAM with LDS/STS and the X/Y/Z pointers, and use PUSH/POP with the stack.
courses.asm:
; Store a byte in SRAM and read it back through X
ldi r26, 0x60   ; XL -> SRAM start
ldi r27, 0x00   ; XH
ldi r16, 0x37
st  X, r16      ; mem[0x60] = 0x37
ld  r18, X      ; r18 = mem[0x60]
out PORTB, r18

lessons.title: The data space map
paragraphs: AVR data memory is one flat address space: 0x00–0x1F are the registers, 0x20–0x5F are I/O registers, and SRAM begins at 0x60. LDS Rd, addr and STS addr, Rr move a byte directly to or from a data address.
This lab's SRAM runs from 0x60 upward; writing there does not disturb the registers.
lessons.pitfall: Addresses below 0x60 alias the registers and I/O; store your data at 0x60 and above.

question.prompt: Where does SRAM start in this model?
question.explanation: 0x60 follows the register and I/O regions.

lessons.title: The X, Y and Z pointers
paragraphs: X (r27:r26), Y (r29:r28) and Z (r31:r30) are 16-bit pointers made of register pairs. LD Rd, X reads the byte they point at; ST X, Rr writes it. X+ post-increments and -X pre-decrements the pointer.
Pointers let one short loop walk an array in SRAM.
lessons.example:
ld r16, X+   ; read, then advance X
st -Y, r17   ; move Y back, then write
lessons.pitfall: Load the pointer's low and high bytes (e.g. r26 and r27 for X) before using it, or it points at address 0.

question.prompt: Which register pair is the Z pointer?

lessons.title: Walking an array
paragraphs: Combining a pointer with post-increment and a DEC/BRNE counter is the standard way to sum or scan an array: load through X+, accumulate, decrement the count, repeat.
The pointer advances automatically, so the loop body stays tiny.
lessons.example:
loop:
  ld r0, X+
  add r16, r0
  dec r18
  brne loop
lessons.pitfall: Post-increment changes the pointer even on the last iteration; that is fine as long as you do not read past your data.

question.prompt: `ld r0, X+` does what to X?

options.text: advances it by one after the read

lessons.title: The stack: PUSH and POP
paragraphs: The stack pointer SP starts at the top of data memory and grows downward. PUSH Rr stores a register and moves SP down; POP Rd moves SP up and restores a register.
Push the registers a routine will clobber, then pop them in reverse order before returning.
lessons.example:
push r16
...
pop r16   ; restores the pushed value
lessons.pitfall: POP in the wrong order returns the wrong values; stacks are last-in, first-out.

question.prompt: The AVR stack grows:

options.text: downward from the top of RAM

steps: Run the preset and find 0x37 at address 0x60 in the memory panel.
Change the stored value and the X pointer and re-run.
Write a loop that fills mem[0x60..0x64] with 1..5 using X+.
PUSH two registers, clobber them, and POP them back.
courses.expected: mem[0x60] = 0x37 and r18 = 0x37; the X pointer addresses SRAM.

bridge.principle: Pointers plus a counter is how assembly walks arrays.
bridge.minecraft: A pointer is a minecart address that moves one block per load.
bridge.other: The same program runs on a real ATmega with avr-gcc/avra and avrdude, or under simulavr; the mnemonics and flags are identical to this subset.

questions.explanation: LD Rd, X+ reads then advances.

courses.title: 24. AVR I/O ports: driving pins
courses.summary: Configure a port with DDRB, write pins with PORTB and set or clear single bits with SBI and CBI.
courses.asm:
; Make PB0 an output and drive it high
sbi DDRB, 0    ; PB0 is an output
sbi PORTB, 0   ; PB0 high
in  r16, PORTB ; read the port back
ldi r17, 0xFF
out DDRB, r17  ; all of port B outputs

lessons.title: Data direction with DDRB
paragraphs: Each port has a direction register (DDRB) and a data register (PORTB). A 1 in DDRB makes that pin an output; a 0 makes it an input. OUT writes a whole byte to an I/O register; IN reads one back.
Set direction first, then drive the data.
lessons.example:
ldi r16, 0xFF
out DDRB, r16  ; all PORTB pins are outputs
lessons.pitfall: Driving PORTB before setting DDRB changes nothing visible; configure direction first.

question.prompt: A 1 bit in DDRB makes that pin:

lessons.title: SBI and CBI
paragraphs: SBI io, b sets bit b of a low I/O register; CBI io, b clears it — a single-instruction read-modify-write that leaves the other pins alone. They work on the lower I/O registers (addresses 0x00–0x1F), which include DDRB and PORTB.
This is how you toggle one LED without disturbing the rest of the port.
lessons.example:
sbi PORTB, 3   ; PB3 high
cbi PORTB, 3   ; PB3 low
lessons.pitfall: SBI/CBI only reach low I/O addresses; a high I/O register needs IN, ORI/ANDI, then OUT.

question.prompt: SBI PORTB, 2 affects:

lessons.title: IN and OUT
paragraphs: OUT io, Rr copies a register to an I/O register; IN Rd, io copies an I/O register into a register. Named ports (PORTB, DDRB, PINB) assemble to their addresses.
To change several bits of a high port at once, read with IN, modify with ANDI/ORI, and write back with OUT.
lessons.example:
in  r16, PINB
ori r16, 0b0001
out PORTB, r16
lessons.pitfall: PINB reads the pins; writing PORTB sets the output latch. Reading and writing use different registers on real hardware.

question.prompt: OUT copies:

options.text: an I/O register into a register
a register into an I/O register

question.explanation: OUT writes a register to an I/O port.

lessons.title: A blink pattern
paragraphs: Firmware blinks an LED by setting the pin's direction once, then alternately setting and clearing the pin inside a loop. In this simulator each PORTB write is recorded as output so you can see the pattern.
On real hardware a delay loop sets the blink rate; here you simply watch the sequence of port values.
lessons.example:
sbi DDRB, 0
loop:
  sbi PORTB, 0
  cbi PORTB, 0
  rjmp loop
lessons.pitfall: Without a delay a real LED would blink too fast to see; the concept and the port writes are what matter here.

question.prompt: To blink PB0 you alternately use:
question.explanation: Set then clear the pin bit.

steps: Run the preset and read DDRB and PORTB in the I/O view.
Add CBI PORTB,0 and watch the recorded output change.
Set all of port B as outputs and drive 0b10101010.
Build a two-step blink loop and read the output list.
courses.expected: DDRB bit0 then all bits set; PORTB bit0 high; r16 reads the PORTB value.

bridge.principle: A direction register and a data register together control a pin.
bridge.minecraft: DDR is whether a lever is wired to drive a lamp; PORT is the lever.
bridge.other: The same program runs on a real ATmega with avr-gcc/avra and avrdude, or under simulavr; the mnemonics and flags are identical to this subset.

courses.title: 25. AVR subroutines and the call stack
courses.summary: Factor code into subroutines with RCALL and RET, and preserve registers across calls with PUSH/POP.
courses.asm:
; Call a routine that doubles r16
  ldi r16, 21
  rcall double
  out PORTB, r16   ; 42
  rjmp end
double:
  lsl r16          ; r16 = r16 * 2
  ret
end:
  nop

lessons.title: RCALL and RET
paragraphs: RCALL label pushes the address of the next instruction onto the stack and jumps to the routine; RET pops that address back into the program counter. This is how one routine can be reused from many places.
A routine ends with RET so control returns to wherever it was called from.
lessons.example:
rcall double
...
double:
  lsl r16
  ret
lessons.pitfall: A routine that falls off the end without RET keeps executing whatever follows; always finish with RET.

question.prompt: RET restores the PC from:
question.explanation: The return address was pushed on the stack.

lessons.title: Preserving registers
paragraphs: A subroutine often needs scratch registers. Push the ones it will modify at entry and pop them in reverse before RET, so the caller's values survive the call.
This simple convention keeps routines composable.
lessons.example:
work:
  push r16
  ...
  pop r16
  ret
lessons.pitfall: Pop in the exact reverse of the push order, or registers come back swapped.

question.prompt: To protect r16 inside a routine you:

options.text: PUSH on entry, POP before RET

question.explanation: Save and restore via the stack.

lessons.title: Passing values
paragraphs: AVR has no built-in argument mechanism; by convention callers pass values in registers (often r24/r25 or r16) and receive results the same way. Agreeing on which registers carry what is a calling convention.
Keeping the convention consistent lets routines call each other reliably.
lessons.example:
ldi r16, 21   ; argument in r16
rcall double  ; result left in r16
lessons.pitfall: If the caller and routine disagree on which register holds the argument, the routine reads garbage.

question.prompt: AVR passes subroutine arguments:
question.explanation: There is no built-in arg passing; use registers by convention.

lessons.title: Nested calls
paragraphs: Because return addresses live on the stack, routines can call other routines; each RCALL pushes and each RET pops, unwinding correctly as long as the stack is balanced.
Deep nesting simply uses more stack.
lessons.example:
a:
  rcall b
  ret
b:
  ret
lessons.pitfall: Unbalanced PUSH/POP inside a routine corrupts the return address and RET jumps somewhere wrong.

question.prompt: Nested calls work because return addresses are:

steps: Run the preset and confirm r16 = 42 after the call.
Step into the routine and watch SP change on RCALL and RET.
Add a second routine and call it from the first.
Give the routine a PUSH/POP pair and verify the caller's register survives.
courses.expected: r16 becomes 42; RCALL pushes the return address, RET pops it.

bridge.principle: The stack turns flat instructions into reusable routines.
bridge.minecraft: RCALL/RET is a minecart that remembers the station it left.
bridge.other: The same program runs on a real ATmega with avr-gcc/avra and avrdude, or under simulavr; the mnemonics and flags are identical to this subset.

courses.title: 26. AVR capstone: a counting LED driver
courses.summary: Combine registers, loops, memory, I/O and a subroutine into a small, tested AVR program.
courses.asm:
; Count 0..3 and show each value on PORTB via a subroutine
  ldi r17, 0xFF
  out DDRB, r17    ; port B all outputs
  ldi r16, 0       ; counter
  ldi r18, 4       ; how many values
loop:
  rcall show
  inc r16
  dec r18
  brne loop
  rjmp end
show:
  out PORTB, r16   ; display the current count
  ret
end:
  nop

lessons.title: Plan the program
paragraphs: Real firmware is built from the pieces you have practiced: set up I/O, keep state in registers, loop a fixed number of times, and factor repeated work into a subroutine.
Decide which register holds the counter, which holds the limit, and what the routine does before you write a line.
lessons.example: r16 = counter, r18 = remaining, show: OUT PORTB, r16
lessons.pitfall: Plan your register use up front; running out of high registers mid-program forces awkward rewrites.

question.prompt: A good first step in an assembly program is to:

lessons.title: Set up the port
paragraphs: The driver makes port B all outputs with OUT DDRB before writing any values, so the pins actually drive. The counter then appears on PORTB each pass.
Configuring direction once at the start is the usual pattern.
lessons.example:
ldi r17, 0xFF
out DDRB, r17
lessons.pitfall: Skipping the DDRB setup means the data writes have no visible effect on hardware.

question.prompt: The driver sets DDRB to 0xFF to:

options.text: make all port B pins outputs

lessons.title: Loop and display
paragraphs: A DEC/BRNE loop runs the body a fixed number of times; each pass calls the show routine and increments the counter. The subroutine keeps the display logic in one place.
Because DEC leaves carry alone, the counter in r16 is unaffected by the loop control in r18.
lessons.example:
loop:
  rcall show
  inc r16
  dec r18
  brne loop
lessons.pitfall: Using the same register for the counter and the loop count would corrupt one of them; keep them separate.

question.prompt: The routine is called with:
question.explanation: RCALL invokes the subroutine each pass.

lessons.title: Verify the result
paragraphs: Run the program and read the recorded PORTB output: it should be 0,1,2,3. The listing shows each instruction's address and opcode, and the registers confirm the final state.
Verifying against an expected sequence is how you know the program is correct, not just that it ran.
lessons.example: expected PORTB writes: 0, 1, 2, 3
lessons.pitfall: A program that 'runs' is not necessarily correct; check the output against what you expected.

question.prompt: You confirm the driver works by:
question.explanation: Compare the output to the expected sequence.

steps: Assemble the capstone and read the full listing.
Run it and confirm the PORTB output is 0,1,2,3.
Change the limit to 8 and predict the new output.
Add a second routine that clears PORTB after the count.
courses.expected: PORTB is driven with 0,1,2,3 in turn; the recorded output is [0,1,2,3] and the loop ends with Z set.

bridge.other: The same program runs on a real ATmega with avr-gcc/avra and avrdude, or under simulavr; the mnemonics and flags are identical to this subset.
